hb.zukan.about.cation: A positively charged ion. The δ− O of water is attracted, and the ion dissolves surrounded by water (hydration).

hb.zukan.about.hclCl: The chloride ion split from HCl.
hb.zukan.about.nonpolar: It has almost no charge separation, so it hardly dissolves in water but dissolves well in a nonpolar solvent like hexane.

hb.page.hydration.title: How hydration works
hb.page.hydration.body:
A water molecule is bent. Its O is slightly negative (δ−) and its H atoms slightly positive (δ+): it is a polar molecule.
Water molecules gather around cations with their O facing in, and around anions with their H facing in. This is hydration, and hydrated ions leave the crystal and spread through the water.
Sodium chloride dissolves because both Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are hydrated and peeled off the crystal.
hb.page.philic.title: Hydrophilic and hydrophobic groups
hb.page.philic.body:
The -OH (hydroxy group) of ethanol C₂H₅OH forms hydrogen bonds with water, so it mixes with water: a hydrophilic group.
The hydrocarbon part such as C₂H₅- does not mix with water: a hydrophobic group.
The larger the share of hydrophilic groups, the more soluble the molecule. Glucose and sucrose, with many -OH groups, dissolve well even though they do not ionize.
hb.page.electrolyte.title: Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes
hb.page.electrolyte.body:
A substance that splits into cations and anions in water (ionizes) is an electrolyte. NaCl and HCl ionize almost completely: strong electrolytes.
Ammonia and acetic acid ionize only partly: weak electrolytes.
Glucose and ethanol dissolve without ionizing: nonelectrolytes. Their solutions hardly conduct electricity.
hb.page.like.title: Like dissolves like
hb.page.like.body:
A very polar solvent (water) dissolves ionic crystals and polar molecules well.
A nonpolar solvent (hexane) dissolves nonpolar molecules like iodine and naphthalene well; nonpolar molecules mix through weak intermolecular forces.
Ions and glucose hardly dissolve in hexane, and iodine hardly dissolves in water. Check it with Experiment 4 in the textbook (copper(II) sulfate, iodine, ethanol, hexane).
hb.page.insoluble.title: Ionic crystals that hardly dissolve
hb.page.insoluble.body:
Not every ionic crystal dissolves well in water. In AgCl, BaSO₄ and CaCO₃ the ions hold each other more strongly than hydration can pull them apart, so they hardly dissolve.
That is why they appear as precipitates when solutions are mixed (e.g. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form a white AgCl precipitate).
BaSO₄ is so insoluble that it is not absorbed by the body, so it is used as a contrast agent for stomach X-rays.

cr.tagline: Change the conditions and watch things dissolve and crystallize
cr.guide1: This is my workshop, with three benches: solids, gases and concentration. Move the conditions as you like and see with your own eyes what changes.
cr.closed: Your teacher has closed this gate
cr.r.hydrateNote: CuSO₄ comes out as the blue pentahydrate. The crystals take water with them, so the water in the solution goes down.
cr.curve.title: Solubility curves
cr.found.title: Discoveries
cr.found.lead: Each new phenomenon earns a {reward} Hiyama discovery reward. Found {n} / {total}.
cr.discover.head: Discovery! "{name}"

cr.d.allDissolvedLine: Below the solubility, everything dissolves. That is unsaturated.
cr.d.allDissolvedHint: Dissolve a little solute in plenty of water
cr.d.saturatedLine: Anything beyond the solubility stays undissolved. With leftover solid, the solution is saturated.
cr.d.saturatedHint: Put a lot of solute into the water
cr.d.precipitateLine: Cooling lowers the solubility, and what can no longer stay dissolved comes out as crystals. That is the basis of recrystallization.
cr.d.precipitateHint: Slowly cool a solution where everything has dissolved
cr.d.redissolveLine: For most solids the solubility rises with temperature. Heat it and the leftover solid dissolves.
cr.d.redissolveHint: Heat a beaker with leftover solid
cr.d.supersatLine: Above the solubility, yet no crystals. Rapid cooling occasionally does this. It is an unstable state.
cr.d.supersatHint: Cool a hot solution very quickly (it happens only sometimes)
cr.d.seedLine: Drop a tiny crystal into a supersaturated solution and crystals grow all at once around it.
cr.d.seedHint: When it becomes supersaturated, drop a seed crystal
cr.d.hydrateWaterLine: Dissolving CuSO₄·5H₂O adds the water inside the crystal (about 36% of its mass) to the solvent.
cr.d.naclFlatLine: The solubility of NaCl hardly changes with temperature, so cooling does not produce many crystals.
cr.d.naclFlatHint: Move the temperature a lot with leftover NaCl
cr.d.mixSeparateLine: The small amount of CuSO₄ stays dissolved, and only KNO₃ crystallizes because of the difference in solubility. That is purification by recrystallization.
cr.d.mixSeparateHint: Dissolve the mixture, then cool it
cr.view.label: View
cr.view.help: Drag with one finger to rotate / pinch with two fingers to zoom / move two fingers to pan / double-tap to reset the view
cr.g.hclNote: HCl is extremely soluble in water and ionizes when it dissolves. Gases like this do not follow Henry's law, so it is not calculated here.
cr.g.released: Gas released when the valve opened: {n}×10⁻³ mol ({v} mL at STP)
cr.g.airNote: Oxygen is {o}% of the dissolved gas (20% in air), because oxygen dissolves in water more easily.
cr.g.unit: One dot in the water = {u}×10⁻³ mol (set for each gas)
cr.c.volLine: Solution {m} g ÷ density {d} g/cm³ = volume {v} mL / amount {n} mol (molar mass {M} g/mol)
cr.d.gasHenryLine: The amount (and mass) of gas that dissolves is proportional to the pressure. But measured at that same pressure, the volume of dissolved gas stays the same.
cr.d.gasHenryHint: Keep the gas, temperature and water the same, and double the pressure
cr.d.gasTempLine: Gas solubility goes down as temperature rises. That is why fish gasp at the surface of warm ponds in summer.
cr.d.gasTempHint: Keep the gas and pressure the same, and change the temperature a lot
cr.d.gasBubblesLine: When the pressure drops, gas that can no longer stay dissolved comes out as bubbles — just like opening a fizzy drink.
cr.d.gasBubblesHint: Raise the pressure to 2.0×10⁵ Pa or more, then open the valve
cr.d.gasAirLine: In a gas mixture, each gas dissolves in proportion to its own partial pressure. Oxygen dissolves more easily than nitrogen, so dissolved air is richer in oxygen.
cr.d.gasHCl: A gas that breaks Henry's law
cr.d.gasHClLine: Gases that are extremely soluble in water, like HCl and NH₃, do not follow Henry's law.
cr.d.concDensityLine: With the same masses of solute and solvent, mass percent and molality stay the same. Density changes the volume of the solution, so only molarity changes.
cr.d.concDensityHint: Leave the solute and solvent alone and move only the density a lot
cr.d.concDiluteLine: In a dilute aqueous solution, 1 L of solution ≈ 1 kg of water, so molarity and molality are almost the same.
cr.d.concDiluteHint: Set the density to 1.00 and make a very dilute solution
cr.d.concScaleLine: Scaling solute and solvent by the same factor does not change the concentration — concentration is a ratio.
cr.d.concScaleHint: Double both the solute and the solvent

cr.o.o03.q: You have 105 g of a saturated KNO₃ solution at 60°C. If all the water evaporates, how many grams of KNO₃ remain? (Solubility at 60°C: {s})
cr.o.o03.how: A {t} g saturated solution (100 g water + {s} g KNO₃) contains {s} g of KNO₃. For 105 g: 105 × {s}/{t} = {r} g.
cr.o.o04.q: A {m} g saturated KNO₃ solution at 60°C is cooled to 20°C. How many grams of KNO₃ crystallize? (Solubility 60°C: {s60}, 20°C: {s20})
cr.o.o04.how: This solution is {s60} g dissolved in 100 g of water. At 20°C only {s20} g can stay dissolved, so {s60} − {s20} = {r} g crystallizes.
cr.o.o05.q: A 100 g saturated KNO₃ solution at 60°C is cooled to 10°C. How many grams crystallize? (Solubility 60°C: {s60}, 10°C: {s10})
cr.o.o05.how: For every {t} g of saturated solution, {d} g ({s60} − {s10}) crystallizes. For 100 g: 100 × {d}/{t} = {r} g.
cr.o.o06.q: A {m} g saturated KCl solution at 80°C is cooled to 0°C. How many grams of KCl crystallize? (Solubility 80°C: {s80}, 0°C: {s0})
cr.o.o06.how: {m} g is 200 g of water + {s80}×2 g of KCl. The difference for 200 g of water is ({s80} − {s0}) × 2 = {r} g.
cr.o.o07.q: 50 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 100 g of water at 60°C. How many grams crystallize at 20°C? (Solubility at 20°C: {s20})
cr.o.o07.how: Even if it is not saturated, the idea is the same. Only {s20} g can stay dissolved at 20°C, so 50 − {s20} = {r} g.
cr.o.o08.q: 100 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 200 g of water at 70°C. How many grams crystallize at 10°C? (Solubility at 10°C: {s10})
cr.o.o08.how: With 200 g of water, {s10} × 2 = {c} g can stay dissolved at 10°C. 100 − {c} = {r} g.
cr.o.o09.q: 64 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 100 g of water at 80°C. As it cools, at what temperature do crystals start to appear? (Read the solubility curve behind the beaker)
cr.o.o09.how: It becomes saturated where the solubility is exactly 64, and crystals appear below that. From the curve: {r}°C.
cr.o.o10.q: 100 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 100 g of water at 80°C. At what temperature do crystals start to appear? (Solubility 50°C: {s50}, 60°C: {s60}; treat the curve as straight between them)
cr.o.o11.q: 40 g of water evaporates at 60°C from a {m} g saturated KNO₃ solution. How many grams crystallize? (Solubility at 60°C: {s})
cr.o.o11.how: What had been dissolved in the 40 g of evaporated water comes out: {s} × 40/100 = {r} g.
cr.o.o12.q: A {m} g saturated NaCl solution at 80°C is cooled to 0°C. How many grams of NaCl crystallize? (Solubility 80°C: {s80}, 0°C: {s0})
cr.o.o12.how: {s80} − {s0} = {r} g. NaCl's solubility barely changes with temperature, so cooling yields very little.
cr.o.o13.q: 50 g of CuSO₄·5H₂O is fully dissolved in 100 g of water at 60°C. How many grams of water are in the solution? (CuSO₄·5H₂O = 250, of which 5H₂O = 90)
cr.o.o13.how: The crystal holds 50 × 90/250 ≈ {w} g of water, which joins the solvent: 100 + {w} = {r} g.
cr.o.o14.q: How many grams of CuSO₄·5H₂O dissolve in 100 g of water at 20°C? (CuSO₄ solubility at 20°C: {s}; CuSO₄ = 160, CuSO₄·5H₂O = 250)
cr.o.o14.how: Dissolving x g gives 160x/250 g of CuSO₄ in 100 + 90x/250 g of water. Solve (160x/250) ÷ (100 + 90x/250) = {s}/100: x ≈ {r} g.
cr.o.o15.q: A {m} g saturated CuSO₄ solution at 60°C is cooled to 10°C. How many grams of CuSO₄·5H₂O crystallize? (CuSO₄ solubility 60°C: {s60}, 10°C: {s10})
cr.o.o15.how: If x g crystallizes, {s60} − 160x/250 g of CuSO₄ stays in 100 − 90x/250 g of water. Set their ratio to {s10}/100: x = {r} g. The key is that the crystals take water with them.
cr.o.o16.q: A mixture of 90 g KNO₃ and 10 g CuSO₄·5H₂O is dissolved in 100 g of water at 60°C and cooled to 10°C. How many grams of KNO₃ crystallize? (Solubility at 10°C — KNO₃: {s10}, CuSO₄: {c10})
cr.o.o16.how: 10 g of CuSO₄·5H₂O adds {w} g of water, so there is 100 + {w} g. All the CuSO₄ ({c} g) stays dissolved. KNO₃ can stay dissolved up to {s10} × (100 + {w})/100 g; subtract from 90 to get {r} g.
cr.o.o17.q: At 0°C and 1.013×10⁵ Pa, {s}×10⁻³ mol of N₂ dissolves in 1 L of water. At 0°C and 3.039×10⁵ Pa, how many mg of N₂ dissolve in 1 L? (N₂ = 28)
cr.o.o17.how: Henry's law: the amount dissolved is proportional to pressure. {s}×10⁻³ × 3 mol × {M} g/mol = {r} mg.
cr.o.o18.q: Same conditions as before (0°C, 3.039×10⁵ Pa, 1 L of water). Measured at that pressure, what volume in mL is the dissolved N₂? ({s}×10⁻³ mol at 1.013×10⁵ Pa)
cr.o.o18.how: The amount triples, but so does the pressure, so the volume at that pressure equals the volume at 1.013×10⁵ Pa: {s}×10⁻³ × 22.4 L ≈ {r} mL.
cr.o.o19.q: Air (N₂ : O₂ = 4 : 1) at 20°C and 1.013×10⁵ Pa touches 10 L of water. How many mg of O₂ dissolve? (O₂: {s}×10⁻³ mol per 1 L of water at 1.013×10⁵ Pa; O₂ = 32)
cr.o.o19.how: O₂'s partial pressure is 1/5 of the total. {s}×10⁻³ × 1/5 × 10 L × 32 = {r} mg. For gas mixtures, use partial pressures.
cr.o.o20.q: 1 L of water in contact with CO₂ at 20°C and 2.026×10⁵ Pa is warmed to 60°C at the same pressure. How much CO₂ comes out, in ×10⁻³ mol? (At 1.013×10⁵ Pa per 1 L — 20°C: {s20}×10⁻³ mol, 60°C: {s60}×10⁻³ mol)
cr.o.o20.how: At double pressure, {s20}×2 dissolves at 20°C and {s60}×2 at 60°C. The difference is ({s20} − {s60}) × 2 = {r}×10⁻³ mol.
cr.o.o21.q: 20 g of NaCl is dissolved in 180 g of water. What is the mass percent concentration?
cr.o.o21.how: The denominator is the mass of the solution (solute + solvent). 20 ÷ (20 + 180) × 100 = {r}%.
cr.o.o22.q: 36 g of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆ = {M}) is dissolved in 250 g of water. What is the molality in mol/kg?
cr.o.o22.how: Amount: 36/{M} = {n} mol. The denominator is the mass of the solvent in kg: {n} ÷ 0.250 = {r} mol/kg.
cr.o.o23.q: A solution of 20 g NaCl in 180 g of water has a density of 1.07 g/cm³. What is the molarity in mol/L? (NaCl = {M})
cr.o.o23.how: Solution volume = 200 g ÷ 1.07 g/cm³ ≈ {v} mL. Amount: 20/{M} ≈ {n} mol. {n} ÷ ({v}/1000) ≈ {r} mol/L.
cr.o.o24.q: Concentrated sulfuric acid is 98% by mass with a density of 1.84 g/cm³. What is its molarity in mol/L? (H₂SO₄ = {M})
cr.o.o24.how: Take 1 L (1000 cm³): mass 1000 × 1.84 = 1840 g, 98% of which is H₂SO₄ = 1803 g; 1803 ÷ {M} ≈ {r} mol. So {r} mol/L.

fz.how.freeze.head: Particles make water harder to freeze
fz.how.freeze.text: At 0℃, water molecules line up neatly and become ice. Mixed-in particles (dissolved substance) get in the way, so it stays liquid at lower temperatures. More particles, lower freezing point.
fz.how.boil.head: Particles make water harder to boil
fz.how.boil.text: Molecules leave the water surface as vapor. Particles make that harder, so the water must go above 100℃ to boil. More particles, higher boiling point.
fz.how.vapor.head: Cloth with many particles dries slowly
fz.how.vapor.text: Water with particles evaporates less (its vapor pressure is lower). That is why clothes wet with seawater dry slowly. Diluting with fresh water helps it dry.
fz.how.osmo.head: Water moves toward the side with more particles
fz.how.osmo.text: Across a membrane that lets only water through (semipermeable), water moves to the side with more particles (osmosis). That push is the osmotic pressure. Press the seawater side harder than it, and water flows back: fresh water (reverse osmosis).
fz.how.mm.head: Same grams, heavier molecules, fewer particles
fz.how.mm.text: How far the freezing point drops depends on the number of particles (mol). For the same 9 g, a substance with a larger molar mass has fewer mol and drops less. So the drop tells you the molar mass.
fz.how.ice.alt: Pure water freezes at 0℃; with particles it does not
fz.how.vapor.alt: With particles, fewer molecules leave the surface
fz.how.osmo.alt: Water crosses the membrane toward the side with particles
fz.how.ionHead: Some substances split into particles in water (ionization)

cl.title: Sekio Rocko-Colloid
cl.tagline: Paths in the mist open with the properties of colloids
cl.closed: Your teacher has closed this gate
cl.guide1: Welcome to the misty lake. The mist here only shows its paths when light shines on it. I'll teach you each tool, one at a time.
cl.area1.name: Misty Cove
cl.area2.name: Shimmering Shoal
cl.area3.name: Cellophane Gate
cl.area4.name: Thunder Shrine
cl.area5.name: Muddy River
cl.area6.name: Tofu Village
cl.area7.name: Ink Library
cl.ruler.head: A ruler for particle size
cl.how1.head: In a colloidal solution, you can see the path of light
cl.how1.text: Shine light from the side: in an ordinary solution (salt water etc.) the light passes straight through and you can't see its path. In a colloidal solution the particles scatter light in all directions, so the path glows. This is the Tyndall phenomenon.
cl.how1.size: Colloid particles are about 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷ m across — bigger than molecules and ions, just the right size to scatter light.
cl.how1.say0: This is the Light Bell. Ring it and light shines from the side. In the cove, the path continues only beyond water where you can see the light's path.
cl.how1.say1: Whether you see it depends on particle size. Remember this ruler — it helps everywhere on this lake.
cl.how2.head: Points of light jiggle around (Brownian motion)
cl.how2.text: Look at a side-lit colloidal solution through the ultramicroscope: the particles appear as points of light moving irregularly. That is because water molecules hit the particles from all directions. This is Brownian motion.
cl.how2.size: Water molecules are too small to see, but colloid particles scatter light, so they show up as points. Big particles like mud barely move when hit and sink.
cl.how2.say0: Next, the Ultra Glasses. Tiny particles you normally can't see appear as points of light.
cl.how2.say1: The particles don't move by themselves. Invisible water molecules push them.
cl.how3.head: Cellophane lets only small particles through (dialysis)
cl.how3.text: Cellophane has very tiny pores. Molecules and ions pass, but colloid particles are too big. Put a colloidal solution in a cellophane bag in water and only the mixed-in ions move out. This is dialysis.
cl.how3.size: Filter paper pores are large, so colloid particles pass through (filtering can't separate them). Cellophane pores are about the size of molecules and ions, so they can separate colloid particles.
cl.how3.say0: The gate's key is a red-brown colloidal solution of iron(III) hydroxide. But H⁺ and Cl⁻ from making it are mixed in, so it's impure.
cl.how3.say1: With the Cellophane Bag you can drive out just the ions. Check the ruler to see why.
cl.pic.tyn.alt: Light from the side shows a path only in the colloidal solution
cl.pic.brown.alt: Water molecules hit a colloid particle from all sides and it zigzags
cl.pic.dial.alt: Only small ions leave the cellophane bag
cl.howProbe: Pick a tool, then tap what you want to check. When you know, mark it "This" and lock in.
cl.howProbeMulti: Check all of them with the tool, mark every one that fits as "This", then lock in.
cl.saw.bell.yes: Look! The light's path glows. The particles inside are scattering the light.
cl.saw.bell.no: The light passes through; no path. The particles are too small.
cl.saw.glasses.none: Nothing shows through the glasses. The particles are too small to scatter light.
cl.saw.glasses.brown: Points of light are jiggling around.
cl.pickMulti: Choose all that apply, then lock in.
cl.q.1-1: Three pools in the cove. The path continues only beyond the pool where you can see the light's path. Check them with the Light Bell.
cl.ok.1-1: Yes, the starch water! A path appeared out of the mist.
cl.learn.1-1: Starch water is a colloidal solution: shine light from the side and you see its path (Tyndall phenomenon). Sugar molecules are too small to scatter light.
cl.q.1-2: Thick mist ahead. There is a bridge, but you can't see it. Ring the Light Bell first.
cl.used.1-2: A sharp beam shows in the mist. Why can you see a beam inside the mist?
cl.opt.1-2.scatter: Mist droplets scatter light in all directions
cl.opt.1-2.emit: Mist droplets give off their own light
cl.ng.1-2.absorb: If they absorbed it, it would get darker. But the beam looks bright.
cl.ng.1-2.emit: Stop the bell and the beam disappears. The droplets don't glow by themselves.
cl.ok.1-2: Right! Scattered light reaches your eyes, so you see the beam. The bridge appeared.
cl.learn.1-2: Mist is a colloid (aerosol): tiny water droplets spread through air (a gas). The droplets scatter light, so you see its path — like sunbeams in a forest.
cl.q.1-3: Three cups before the shrine. Choose every cup where the light's path shows, and the door opens.
cl.ok.1-3: Soapy water and milk! Both are colloids.
cl.learn.1-3: Soapy water (micelles of soap molecules) and milk (fat droplets) are colloids — they are all around us. In salt water, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are too small to scatter light.
cl.why.sugar: Sugar water showed no light path. Sugar molecules are too small.
cl.why.water: Plain water just lets the light pass through.
cl.why.salt: The ions in salt water are too small to scatter light. No path, right?
cl.why.mud: Muddy water is cloudy, but its particles are too big. They didn't jiggle.
cl.why.missing: Not enough yet. Did another one show the light's path?
cl.why.probeFirst: You picked one you haven't checked. Check it with a tool first.
cl.q.2-1: The shoal water is a little cloudy. Look through the Ultra Glasses.
cl.used.2-1: Points of light jiggle irregularly. Why do you think?
cl.opt.2-1.hit: Water molecules around them hit the particles from all sides
cl.opt.2-1.swim: The particles are alive and swim
cl.opt.2-1.light: The light we shine is shaking
cl.ng.2-1.swim: The particles aren't living. Non-living particles move the same way.
cl.ng.2-1.light: Even with steady light, the points keep moving.
cl.ok.2-1: Yes! Invisible water molecules push them. I drew the water molecules in the glasses too. Stepping stones rose up.
cl.learn.2-1: The irregular motion of colloid particles is Brownian motion. It happens because water molecules in thermal motion hit the particles irregularly from all sides.
cl.q.2-2: The shoal stones are carved with particle sizes. Tap them from smallest to largest and the stones line up.
cl.howOrder: Tap from the smallest. You can look at the ruler.
cl.ng.2-2.order: The order seems off. Read the ruler from the left (small).
cl.ok.2-2: That's the order! The stones lined up.
cl.learn.2-2: Molecules, ions (about 10⁻¹⁰ m) < colloid particles (10⁻⁹–10⁻⁷ m) < mud and precipitate. A solution with colloid particles spread through it is a colloidal solution.
cl.q.2-3: The last cups before the far shore. Look through the glasses and choose the one cup where points of light jiggle.
cl.ok.2-3: The iron(III) hydroxide. You'll meet it again at the next gate.
cl.learn.2-3: Iron(III) hydroxide here is a colloidal solution, so you see Brownian motion. Salt water's particles are too small to see; mud's are too big and sink.
cl.q.3-1: You want to get only H⁺ and Cl⁻ out of the gate key (iron(III) hydroxide colloid). Which bag?
cl.ng.3-1.poly: Polyethylene has no pores. Even ions can't get out.
cl.ng.3-1.cloth: Filter paper pores are too big. The colloid particles would leak out too.
cl.ok.3-1: Cellophane. Its pores are just about the size of molecules and ions.
cl.learn.3-1: A membrane like cellophane that lets small molecules and ions through but not colloid particles is a semipermeable membrane. Purifying a colloid with one is dialysis.
cl.q.3-2: Put the bag in water. What moves out? Choose all that apply.
cl.ng.3-2.FeOH: Colloid particles are bigger than cellophane pores. They stay in the bag.
cl.ng.3-2.missing: There is one more ion that goes out.
cl.ok.3-2: Exactly. Only the small ions go out. Through the glasses it looks like this.
cl.learn.3-2: H⁺ and Cl⁻ are small, so they pass through cellophane. The big colloid particles stay in the bag.
cl.q.3-3: Time to purify the key. Bring the ions in the bag down to {n} or less and the key will glow.
cl.dial.start: First, put the cellophane bag with the key liquid into the tub of water.
cl.dial.inDone: The bag is in the water. Wait a bit and ions will move out.
cl.dial.how: "Wait" and ions move out. It stops when inside and outside are equally concentrated, so "Change the water" to make them move out again. Pour it on the key at {n} or less.
cl.dial.waiting: Ions are passing out through the cellophane…
cl.dial.waited: Inside and outside are about equal now, so it stopped. Try changing the outside water.
cl.dial.changed: Fresh water now. Wait again and more ions will move out.
cl.dial.cloudy: The outside water turned white! That's a silver chloride (AgCl) precipitate — proof that Cl⁻ came out.
cl.dial.clearButWait: The outside water stays clear. But there should still be ions in the bag. Wait, then test.
cl.dial.clear: It no longer turns cloudy. Hardly any ions are left.
cl.dial.notYet: There are still {n} ions in the bag. The key is still cloudy.
cl.ok.3-3: The key glows bamboo green! The gate opens.
cl.learn.3-3: Changing the outside water again and again leaves fewer and fewer ions until only colloid particles remain (dialysis). If silver nitrate turns the water white, Cl⁻ has come out.
cl.scope.brownMol: Blue dots = water molecules, hitting from all sides
cl.scope.dialysis: Dotted line = cellophane; left is inside the bag
cl.bye1: The path of light tells you whether it's a colloid. That bell is yours now.
cl.bye2: You can now see even the work of invisible water molecules.
cl.bye3: You purified a colloid by dialysis. Next is the Thunder Shrine — see how the sky is changing?
cl.cap: You have reached today's reward limit, so no reward
cl.already: You already received this area's reward
cl.area8.name: Lake Shrine
cl.shrineDone: You solved the Lake Shrine with all 7 tools!
cl.bye4: A particle's charge decides which way it moves. The electrodes are yours.
cl.bye5: Opposite charge, higher valence. The muddy river holds no fear now.
cl.bye6: Sol, gel, xerogel. You're a tofu master.
cl.bye7: Hydrophilic colloids protect hydrophobic ones. The library's ink is safe.
cl.bye8: You've mastered all 7 tools. The colloid paths of this lake are yours.
cl.how4.head: With electricity, colloid particles move (electrophoresis)
cl.how4.text: Colloid particles are charged either positive or negative. Put in electrodes and apply a voltage, and the particles move toward the electrode of opposite charge. Iron(III) hydroxide is positive, so it moves to the cathode (−); clay is negative, so it moves to the anode (+).
cl.how4.size: Particles of the same kind carry the same charge, so they repel each other and stay spread out instead of clumping. That is one reason colloids don't settle.
cl.how4.say0: Welcome to the Thunder Shrine. With these Twin Electrodes you can move charged particles.
cl.how4.say1: + goes to −, − goes to +. Think of magnets.
cl.how5.head: Ions of opposite charge make colloids settle (coagulation)
cl.how5.text: Add a little electrolyte to a hydrophobic colloid (iron(III) hydroxide, clay etc.) and the particles' charge is cancelled, so they clump and settle. This is coagulation. Ions with the opposite charge and higher valence work with smaller amounts.
cl.how5.size: Hydrophilic colloids (gelatin, starch etc.) hold many water molecules around them, so a little electrolyte doesn't make them settle. A large amount does — this is salting out.
cl.how5.say0: The muddy river flows with particles spread through it. Settle them with the Electrolyte Vials and the riverbed path appears.
cl.how5.say1: Negative ions for positive particles, positive ions for negative ones. The higher the valence, the better.
cl.how6.head: Flowing sol, set gel, dried xerogel
cl.how6.text: A colloidal solution that flows is a sol; a sol that has lost its fluidity and set is a gel. Add nigari to soy milk (sol) and it becomes tofu (gel). A dried gel is a xerogel — like freeze-dried tofu or silica gel.
cl.how6.size: In a gel, colloid particles link into a network holding water in its gaps. Remove the water and you get a porous xerogel.
cl.how6.say0: In Tofu Village everyone makes tofu. Take this Nigari.
cl.how6.say1: Tell sol from gel by whether it flows or has set.
cl.how7.head: Hydrophilic colloids protect hydrophobic ones (protective colloid)
cl.how7.text: Add a hydrophilic colloid to a hydrophobic one and it wraps the particles, so a little electrolyte no longer coagulates them. A hydrophilic colloid acting this way is a protective colloid. In sumi ink, glue (hydrophilic) protects the carbon particles (hydrophobic).
cl.how7.size: Animal glue is related to gelatin. It attracts many water molecules, so even when salt ions come, the particles hardly stick together.
cl.how7.say0: The old scrolls in the Ink Library are written in sumi. Carry the carbon particles safely with the Glue Shield.
cl.how7.say1: The shield is a water-loving hydrophilic colloid — a protective colloid.
cl.how8.head: Solve the Lake Shrine with 7 tools
cl.how8.text: The Lake Shrine has 7 scenes, each with a mechanism. Read each scene and choose the tool that fits best: Light Bell, Ultra Glasses, Cellophane Bag, Twin Electrodes, Electrolyte Vials, Nigari, Glue Shield — all tools you've mastered.
cl.how8.size: Every tool comes from the size of colloid particles (10⁻⁹–10⁻⁷ m), their charge, and their relationship with water.
cl.how8.say0: At last, the Lake Shrine. Light the 7 lamps before dawn.
cl.how8.say1: If you get stuck, remember particle size and charge.
cl.pic.el.alt: Positive particles move to the cathode
cl.pic.el.cap: Positive particles are drawn to the cathode
cl.pic.co.alt: Ions of opposite charge make particles clump and settle
cl.pic.co.cap: Charge cancelled: they clump and settle
cl.pic.pr.alt: Carbon wrapped in glue does not clump
cl.pic.sh.alt: The 7 tools and the Lake Shrine
cl.use.pole: Connect the electrodes and apply voltage
cl.used.4-1: The particles move toward one electrode. These particles are positively charged. Which way did they go?
cl.q.4-1: The shrine's tank holds an iron(III) hydroxide colloid. First, connect the electrodes.
cl.ng.4-1.anode: + and + repel. Positive particles are drawn to the opposite charge.
cl.ng.4-1.stay: Look closely — the particles do move to one side.
cl.ok.4-1: Yes, to the cathode! Positive particles are pulled by the negative electrode.
cl.learn.4-1: Colloid particles moving toward the electrode of opposite charge is electrophoresis. Iron(III) hydroxide particles are positive, so they move to the cathode.
cl.q.4-2: You want a stepping bridge on the left bank. To gather the positive particles on the left, where does the cathode (−) go?
cl.el.how: Choose how to connect the electrodes, then apply voltage.
cl.el.wrong: The particles went right. Positive particles gather at the cathode — put the cathode on the left.
cl.ok.4-2: The particles gathered on the left and made footing!
cl.learn.4-2: Positively charged particles gather at the cathode. Change how the electrodes are connected and you change where they gather.
cl.q.4-3: Next, a clay colloid. Clay particles are negatively charged. Apply voltage — which way do they move?
cl.ng.4-3.cathode: Negative particles and a negative electrode repel.
cl.ng.4-3.stay: Charged particles move when voltage is applied.
cl.ok.4-3: Exactly! Negative particles go to the anode. Watch the tank.
cl.learn.4-3: Colloids of clay and metal sulfides are negatively charged and move to the anode. Electrophoresis tells you the sign of a particle's charge.
cl.q.5-1: Upstream: iron(III) hydroxide cloudiness (positive colloid). Which vial settles it with the smallest amount?
cl.q.5-2: Downstream: clay cloudiness (negative colloid). Which vial settles it with the smallest amount?
cl.ng.5-1.KI: What works is the ion opposite to the particles (negative). I⁻ is −1. Which negative ion has a higher valence?
cl.ng.5-1.CaCl2: Ca²⁺ is positive — same sign as the particles, so they stay repelling. Only Cl⁻ (−1) helps.
cl.ng.5-1.AlNO3: Al³⁺ is positive — same sign as the particles, so it doesn't help. NO₃⁻ is −1.
cl.ng.5-2.Na2SO4: What works is the ion opposite to the particles (positive). Na⁺ is +1. Which positive ion has a higher valence?
cl.ng.5-2.KI: K⁺ is +1. There's a positive ion with a higher valence.
cl.ng.5-2.CaCl2: Ca²⁺ (+2) works, but there's a positive ion with an even higher valence.
cl.ok.5-1: Na₂SO₄! SO₄²⁻ cancelled the positive charge and the cloudiness settled.
cl.ok.5-2: Al(NO₃)₃! Al³⁺ gathered the negative particles and settled them. The riverbed path appears.
cl.learn.5-1: For a positive colloid, negative ions with high valence work best (SO₄²⁻ > Cl⁻, I⁻, NO₃⁻).
cl.learn.5-2: For a negative colloid, positive ions with high valence work best (Al³⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Na⁺, K⁺). Water treatment plants use alum (Al³⁺) to settle river cloudiness the same way.
cl.q.5-3: Left: iron(III) hydroxide (hydrophobic). Right: gelatin (hydrophilic). Add a little electrolyte, then a lot, and compare.
cl.dose.how: Try both "A little" and "A lot", then answer.
cl.dose.saw.little: Just a little made the iron(III) hydroxide settle. The gelatin didn't change.
cl.dose.saw.much: With a lot, the gelatin finally settled too.
cl.opt.5-3.much: Add a large amount of electrolyte
cl.opt.5-3.bag: Wrap it in a cellophane bag
cl.ng.5-3.little: With a little, the gelatin didn't settle.
cl.ng.5-3.bag: Cellophane is for removing ions; it can't settle anything.
cl.ok.5-3: Right. Hydrophilic colloids settle with a lot of electrolyte. That's salting out.
cl.learn.5-3: Hydrophilic colloids hold many water molecules, so a little electrolyte doesn't settle them. A large amount makes them precipitate (salting out).
cl.q.6-1: Soy milk, tofu and koya tofu are on the stand. Which is sol, gel, xerogel?
cl.match.how: Choose one word for each, then lock in.
cl.ng.6-1.tonyu: Soy milk flows freely. What do we call a colloid that flows?
cl.ng.6-1.tofu: Tofu doesn't flow; it has set, but it holds lots of water.
cl.ng.6-1.koya: Koya tofu is tofu frozen and dried. What is a dried gel?
cl.ok.6-1: Perfect! Soy milk → tofu → koya tofu is sol → gel → xerogel.
cl.learn.6-1: A flowing colloidal solution is a sol; one that has set is a gel; a dried gel is a xerogel.
cl.q.6-2: Choose every gel among the village foods.
cl.ng.6-2.milk: Milk flows. Something that flows is a sol.
cl.ng.6-2.tonyu: Soy milk flows. Something that flows is a sol.
cl.ng.6-2.missing: There are more. Which foods are set and wobbly?
cl.learn.6-2: Jelly, konnyaku, tofu and agar are gels. Milk and soy milk are sols — sols and gels are in everyday food.
cl.q.6-3: Add nigari (mainly MgCl₂) to soy milk and it becomes tofu. What is the nigari doing?
cl.opt.6-3.coag: Gathering the protein particles in soy milk so it sets
cl.opt.6-3.dissolve: Dissolving the protein to make it runny
cl.ng.6-3.dissolve: If it got runny, it wouldn't become tofu.
cl.ok.6-3: Yes! The ions in nigari gather the protein particles and set them.
cl.learn.6-3: Ions such as Mg²⁺ in nigari gather the protein colloid particles in soy milk into tofu (a gel) — gathering colloids with electrolytes, like coagulation and salting out.
cl.q.7-1: The sumi ink of the old scrolls contains animal glue. What is the glue for?
cl.opt.7-1.protect: To wrap the carbon particles so they don't clump and settle
cl.ng.7-1.color: The carbon particles give the color. The glue protects them.
cl.ng.7-1.smell: Not for smell — it protects the particles.
cl.ok.7-1: Exactly. The glue is a shield for the carbon particles.
cl.learn.7-1: The carbon particles in sumi are a hydrophobic colloid and coagulate easily. The hydrophilic glue wraps them so they resist coagulation.
cl.q.7-2: Salt mist fills the library corridor. Test the two inks with the Electrolyte Vials and choose the one that can get through.
cl.saw.vial.sink: With electrolyte, the carbon particles clumped and settled at once.
cl.saw.vial.stay: Even with electrolyte, the particles stay spread. The glue protects them.
cl.why.carbon: The carbon-only liquid clumped and settled with salt.
cl.ok.7-2: The sumi ink with glue. Its particles were protected in the salt mist.
cl.learn.7-2: Carbon without glue coagulates with a little electrolyte. With glue (a protective colloid) it resists.
cl.q.7-3: The last bookshelf. Which acts as a protective colloid?
cl.ng.7-3.feoh: Iron(III) hydroxide is hydrophobic — it's the one being protected.
cl.ng.7-3.carbon: Carbon is hydrophobic — it's the one being protected.
cl.ok.7-3: Gelatin! A hydrophilic colloid like animal glue.
cl.learn.7-3: Hydrophilic colloids such as gelatin, animal glue and gum arabic act as protective colloids.
cl.shrine.how: Choose the tool that best fits the scene.
cl.q.8-1: Mist hides the approach to the shrine. You want to make the path's shape appear in the mist.
cl.ok.8-1: The bell's light is scattered by the mist and the path appears!
cl.learn.8-1: Tyndall phenomenon: colloid particles scatter light, so you see its path.
cl.q.8-2: Tiny glowing points tremble in the sacred water. Are they alive, or just particles?
cl.ok.8-2: Through the glasses: particles pushed by water molecules!
cl.learn.8-2: Brownian motion: water molecules hit colloid particles from all sides.
cl.q.8-3: The sacred water (a red-brown colloid) is impure with ions. Remove just the ions.
cl.ok.8-3: In the bag in water, only the ions went out!
cl.learn.8-3: Dialysis: cellophane passes ions but not colloid particles.
cl.q.8-4: Draw footing of positively charged particles to the far bank to build a bridge.
cl.ok.8-4: With the cathode on the far bank, the particles gathered. A bridge!
cl.learn.8-4: Electrophoresis: charged particles move to the electrode of opposite charge.
cl.q.8-5: The basin water is cloudy with clay (a negative colloid). Settle it.
cl.ok.8-5: With the Al³⁺ vial, the cloudiness settled!
cl.learn.8-5: Coagulation: ions of opposite charge and higher valence settle it best.
cl.q.8-6: You want to offer the soy milk as tofu.
cl.ok.8-6: With nigari, the soy milk (sol) became tofu (gel)!
cl.q.8-7: You want to write on the shrine's plaque in sumi, but salt mist blows in from the sea. Protect the ink.
cl.ok.8-7: The Glue Shield protects the ink and glowing characters appear on the plaque! The shrine doors open…
cl.learn.8-7: Protective colloid: a hydrophilic colloid wraps a hydrophobic one so it resists coagulation.

cr.ex.title: See the problem animated
cr.ex.ask: What is the answer in {u}? (The bar, beaker and graph move together.)
cr.ex.tip.solid: The curve is the most that dissolves in 100 g of water. Whatever the glowing point rises above the curve comes out as crystals.
cr.ex.tip.gas: Gases dissolve more at higher pressure and in more water, and less at higher temperature (the line).
cr.ex.tip.conc: More solute makes it stronger. What you divide by (solution? solvent? volume?) decides the kind of concentration.
cr.hint.max: Solubility = the most grams that dissolve in 100 g of water. If the water is not 100 g: solubility × water (g) ÷ 100.
cr.hint.evapAll: If all the water evaporates, everything dissolved comes out. First find how much solute is in this saturated solution: (100 + solubility) g of solution holds solubility g.
cr.hint.cool: Dissolved before cooling − the limit at the cooled temperature = crystals. Read both heights on the graph.
cr.hint.coolSat: "100 g of saturated solution" is not 100 g of water! (100 + solubility) g of solution holds solubility g. Work per (100 + solubility) g, then scale to 100 g.
cr.hint.startT: Convert the dissolved amount to "per 100 g of water" — that is the height on the graph. The temperature where that height meets the curve is the answer.
cr.hint.evap: At the same temperature, the remaining water still holds the same amount. What the lost water held (solubility × lost water ÷ 100) comes out.
cr.hint.hydWater: CuSO₄·5H₂O contains water (90 g in 250 g). When it dissolves, that water joins the solvent.
cr.hint.hydDissolve: Think about both the CuSO₄ inside the hydrate and the water it adds. Compare with the graph (anhydrous solubility) to see if it all dissolves.
cr.hint.hydCool: The crystals are the pentahydrate (they take water with them). First estimate how much would come out as anhydrous salt.
cr.hint.mix: When a mixture cools, only the part over its limit comes out. Check KNO₃ and CuSO₄ separately against their curves.
cr.hint.gasP: Henry's law: the amount (mass) dissolved is proportional to pressure. 3× the pressure → 3× as much.
cr.hint.gasVol: Measured at the pressure it dissolved under, the dissolved gas has the same volume whatever the pressure.
cr.hint.gasAir: For a gas mixture, use each gas's partial pressure. O₂ is 1/5 of the total. 10 L of water → 10×.
cr.hint.gasT: Warmer water holds less gas. Dissolved before − dissolved after warming = gas released. Remember the pressure is 2×.
cr.hint.percent: Mass percent = solute ÷ solution × 100. Solution = solute + solvent (not just the water).
cr.hint.molality: Molality = mol of solute ÷ kg of solvent. g → mol: divide by molar mass. g → kg: divide by 1000.
cr.hint.molarity: Molarity = mol of solute ÷ L of solution. Solution volume = solution mass ÷ density (mL).
cr.hint.molarityDens: Think of 1 L (1000 mL) of solution: mass = 1000 × density, and 98% of that is solute.
fz.anim.head.fp: As the particle concentration m rises, the freezing point keeps dropping
fz.anim.head.bp: As the particle concentration m rises, the boiling point keeps rising
fz.anim.head.vp: Adding fresh water lowers the particle concentration m
fz.anim.head.os: As the concentration c rises, the osmotic pressure Π grows
fz.anim.head.mm: The bigger the molar mass M, the fewer the particles, and the less the freezing point drops
fz.anim.cap.fp: If m (mol of particles per 1 kg of water) doubles, Δt (the drop) doubles too. K_f = 1.85 means "m = 1 lowers it by 1.85 K". Watch the glowing numbers move together.
fz.anim.cap.bp: If m doubles, Δt (the rise) doubles too. K_b = 0.515 means "m = 1 raises it by 0.515 K".
fz.anim.cap.vp: The particles n stay the same, but as the water W grows, m = n ÷ W shrinks. At 0.60 or below, it dries.
fz.anim.cap.os: Π = cRT. At the same temperature, doubling c doubles Π. For electrolytes, count c by particles (ions).
fz.anim.cap.mm: Even with the same 9.0 g, a bigger M means fewer mol (particles). So get mol from Δt, then M = g ÷ mol.
